subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage:
The printer jammed twenty minutes before the client call, and half the office started talking at once. Zeynep, the senior analyst, watched Pablo, who had joined only eight months ago, quietly unplug it, print the deck from his laptop at the other machine, and say to everyone, "Twelve minutes. Who takes slide one?" His voice never rose.

Later, Zeynep found him in the kitchen. "I've been in this job six years and I panic more than you do. How did you stay so steady?"

Pablo laughed, surprised. "I write the worst case on a sticky note. Then it's usually smaller than my head says."

"That's useful. I'm stealing it." She paused. "Next quarter's supplier pitch, I'd like you to lead the first half. I'll sit beside you."

Pablo grinned. "Really?"

qa.q: What did Pablo do when the printer jammed?
qa.a: Pablo unplugged the printer, printed the deck from his laptop at another machine and asked who would take slide one.

qa.q: Why did Zeynep ask Pablo how he stayed so steady?
qa.a: Zeynep admired his calm under pressure and admitted she panics more than he does, so she wanted to learn from him despite his lower rank.

qa.q: What small step could Zeynep take to keep learning from Pablo?
qa.a: She could try his sticky-note habit on her next stressful day and tell Pablo how it went.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel about being offered the first half of the pitch?
qa.a: Pablo probably felt surprised and pleased, since a senior colleague was trusting him with a stretch task and treating his method as worth borrowing.

grounding: Zeynep admires a junior's handling of pressure, tells him so, offers a stretch chance, and learns from him regardless of rank.

passage:
The caller at the Hyderabad support centre had been shouting for eleven minutes about a double charge, and Vidya, the team lead, was listening in on the line. Madhuri, eight months into the job, didn't raise her voice once. She repeated his words back, apologised for the stress, and read out the reversal reference slowly twice. By the end he said, "Sorry for shouting, ma'am."
Vidya took off her headset and sat still. Five years in, she still got flustered on calls like that.
At the break she found Madhuri at the tea machine. "That call was one of the best I've heard. You stayed so calm. I learned something today."
Madhuri laughed nervously. "Really?"
"Really. Next week I'd like you to run the training session on difficult calls. For the whole floor, including the seniors."
Madhuri stared. "Including you?"
"Especially me."

qa.q: How long had the caller been shouting?
What was Vidya feeling as she sat still after taking off her headset?
qa.a: She felt admiration for Madhuri and a little humbled, since she still got flustered on calls like that after five years.

qa.q: How did Vidya turn her admiration into action?
qa.a: She told Madhuri directly and asked her to run the training on difficult calls for the whole floor, seniors included.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to hear this from her team lead?
qa.a: Madhuri is nervous and surprised, then likely proud and encouraged to be trusted with teaching the seniors.

grounding: The protagonist admires a junior's calm under pressure, tells her, gives her a stretch chance, and learns from her regardless of rank.

subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage:
"Hemant, how did you stay so steady last night?"
"Sir? The server outage?"
"Yogesh is fine. And yes. Two hours down, the client calling every ten minutes, and you were the one saying 'Okay, next step.' I was pacing."
Hemant scratched his head. "Honestly, I was scared. I just wrote everything on the whiteboard so I wouldn't forget."
"That whiteboard is the reason we got it back. I've been doing this eight years and I've never thought of doing that."
"It's just a habit from college."
"It's a good one. Can you write it up as a checklist for the team? And I'd like you to lead the post-mortem call on Friday."
"Me? With the client?"
"With the client. I'll be there. But it's your call."
Hemant's grin was slow and wide. "Okay. Yes."
Yogesh picked up a marker. "Show me how you set it out."

qa.q: What did Hemant write on the whiteboard during the outage?
qa.a: Everything, so he wouldn't forget the steps.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling during the outage, and how does he feel about Hemant now?
qa.a: Yogesh was anxious and pacing, and now feels real admiration for how steady Hemant stayed.

qa.q: How did Yogesh show respect for Hemant's skill?
qa.a: He praised him directly, asked him to write a team checklist, and gave him the chance to lead the post-mortem call with the client.

qa.q: How might Hemant see his senior asking him to show the whiteboard method?
qa.a: Hemant is likely surprised and proud that someone with eight years of experience wants to learn from him.

grounding: The protagonist admires a junior's calm under pressure, tells him so, gives a stretch chance, and learns from him despite the gap in rank.
